Two of the longer pages were also cut off: Ellicott's chapter page stops at v. 19 and the Pulpit Commentary's at v. 15. Where I have notes after those points, they come from the verse-by-verse pages on biblehub and studylight. The quotes below are mostly older writers (Harrison, Kidner, Feinberg and others) as quoted by Guzik or the Pulpit Commentary, not their own books.

**Main abbreviations and URLs**
- EW = Enduring Word (David Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-46/
- ELL = Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/46.htm
- PUL = Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/46.htm

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Ellicott: Jeremiah's prophecies about the other nations were gathered into an appendix. Most of them fill out the outline in Jer 25:15–26 and date from Jehoiakim's reign. (ELL)
- Pulpit: "against the Gentiles" is better translated "concerning the nations." This heading covers all seven oracles in chapters 46–49. (PUL)
- Guzik quotes Harrison: Jeremiah starts with Egypt because Palestine had long been under Egypt's political influence. He quotes Trapp: Egypt had recently killed good King Josiah. (EW)

**v. 2**
- Ellicott gives background on Necho II, including his Nile–Red Sea canal project and his killing of Josiah at Megiddo. He dates the Carchemish defeat to about 606 BC and reads the poem as a song of triumph over Egypt the oppressor, sung before it happened. (ELL)
- Guzik dates the battle to 605 BC. He calls it the moment Babylon became the superpower, and says the battle was still in the future when Jeremiah spoke. (EW)
- Pulpit:
  - George Smith identified the site of Carchemish (Jerabis, on the Euphrates).
  - It rejects M. Niebuhr's attempt to make "the fourth year" date the prophecy rather than the battle.
  - It argues the oracle was written at about the time of the battle. (PUL)

**vv. 3–4**
- Who is giving the orders? The commentators disagree:
  - Ellicott: the call goes out to Nebuchadnezzar's army, first the foot soldiers, then the horse, then light troops. He also explains the old word "brigandine" (a light coat of mail). (ELL)
  - Pulpit: Egypt's own leaders are calling their men to arms. It explains the small shield (magen) and the large one covering the whole body (tsinnah), and Egypt's fame for war chariots. (PUL)
- Guzik quotes Cundall: Jeremiah sets Egypt's well-equipped, boastful army against its shameful defeat, with irony. (EW)

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: it seems unbelievable that such a well-equipped army would run, hence the astonished question. "Look not back" means they do not stop to regroup. (PUL)
- Ellicott: "Fear on every side" (Magor-missabib) is one of Jeremiah's signature phrases (6:25; 20:3, 10; 49:29). (ELL)

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: "Let not the swift flee" is a strong way of saying even the swiftest cannot escape. The Jews were struck by how fast the Chaldeans moved. "They have stumbled" is a prophetic perfect, meaning a certain future, though Ewald disagreed and dated the oracle after the battle. (PUL)
- Guzik: Jeremiah pictures Babylonian captains ordering their men to pursue. (EW)
- Expositor's Bible: here the irony turns into an outright curse. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/jeremiah/46.htm)

**vv. 7–8**
- Ellicott:
  - The Hebrew word for "flood" (ye'or) is used almost only of the Nile, so the question already hints at the answer.
  - The "rivers" are the Nile's branches and canals.
  - He compares the scene to an English poet looking back on the Spanish Armada. (ELL)
- Pulpit quotes Ewald's picture of a monstrous river rolling over the lands. It says "the city" in v. 8 means cities in general. (PUL)
- Gill: Pharaoh was reaching for universal monarchy. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/46-8.html)
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): the Nile rises gently but churns where it meets the sea. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-8.htm)

**v. 9**
- The allies: Cush is Ethiopia and Put is an African people. Who the Ludim were is disputed:
  - Ellicott suggests Greek (Ionian and Carian) settlers whom Psammetichus brought into Egypt. (ELL)
  - Pulpit notes Sayce's view that they were Lydian mercenaries. It identifies Put as the Somali coast (following Brugsch) and describes how the Egyptian army was organised. (PUL)
  - Keil & Delitzsch take them as African Lydians. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-8.htm)
- "Come up, ye horses" probably means "prance," not "mount," with echoes of Nahum. (PUL; Keil at the same biblehub URL)
- Guzik: God summons proud Egypt to battle in order to judge it. (EW)

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: Jeremiah draws on Isa 34:8, Zeph 1:7 and Deut 32:42. Egypt's army is the sacrificial victim and the Euphrates bank is the altar. (ELL)
- Pulpit: "the day of the LORD" is God stepping in to set wrongs right. There are many such "days" and yet only one, since each great upheaval is a stage of the final judgment. The sword is "the sword of the LORD" (cf. Isa 34:6; Ezek 39:17–20). (PUL)
- Guzik: this shows that "the day of the LORD" is not always one single day; it can be any time God's power shows itself in judgment. (EW)

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: the verse is triumphant irony. "Virgin" means not yet conquered, and Egypt's monarchy never recovered from this blow. (ELL)
- Pulpit: literally "there is no plaster for thee." (PUL)
- Gill: true balsam grew near Jericho, not in Gilead. The command is figurative: Egypt will raise troops and find allies, all in vain. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/46-11.html)
- Guzik quotes Harrison: "many medicines" is sarcasm. (EW)

**v. 12**
- Gill offers two readings. Either Egyptian and Chaldean warriors fall together, or, as he prefers, Egyptians running away trip over one another. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-12.htm)
- Pulpit: "the land" is better translated "the earth." (PUL)

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: this is a separate, later prophecy, perhaps linked to 43:10. (ELL)
- Pulpit has a long note on whether Nebuchadnezzar ever invaded Egypt:
  - Grote doubted it.
  - Pulpit at first suggested the prophets may have misjudged the timing, and that Cambyses may have been the one who fulfilled it.
  - A later postscript reports Wiedemann's discovery of an inscription. Together with cuneiform records, it describes a campaign in Nebuchadnezzar's 37th year (568–7 BC), which Pulpit takes as confirmation. (PUL)

**v. 14**
- Kidner, quoted by Guzik: these are frontier towns in the path of an invader. (EW)
- Pulpit: translate "the sword hath devoured those round about thee," meaning Egypt's neighbours have already fallen. (PUL)
- Matthew Henry: Jewish refugees had settled in exactly these towns, against God's command. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_046.cfm)

**v. 15**
- Ellicott and Pulpit both prefer the singular, "thy strong one." The Septuagint reads "Why did Apis flee?", making the verse about the sacred bull. On this reading the God of Israel triumphs over Egypt's animal-god, and Ellicott points to Cambyses later killing the bull. (ELL; PUL)
- Expositor's: Apis must give way to Jehovah. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/jeremiah/46.htm)
- Matthew Henry: the warriors were swept away as by a driving rain, because God drove them. (MHC URL above)

**v. 16**
- Who is speaking? Ellicott suggests foreign settlers in Egypt, or the Judean fugitives of 43:5–7. (ELL)
- Ellicott on the ancient translations: the Septuagint reads "the Greek sword" and the Vulgate "the sword of the dove." (ELL)
- Feinberg, quoted by Guzik: mercenaries decide to go home. (EW)
- Biblehub's study notes draw the lesson that escaping judgment comes through repentance, not moving somewhere else. (https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/46-16.htm)

**v. 17**
- Ellicott's preferred rendering: "They have called Pharaoh's name, A Noise; he hath passed the appointed season," meaning the time God's patience allowed him. He also lists the ancient and Reformation readings: the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and Luther's "he has left his tent." (ELL)
- Barnes: this is a prophetic nickname, like Magor-missabib. Pharaoh's boasts proved empty. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-17.htm)
- Matthew Poole gives several options for who is mocking Pharaoh and what "time" he missed. (same URL)
- Coffman: the mercenaries are the speakers. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/46-17.html)
- Guzik quotes Harrison ("Loudmouth") and Kidner ("Noisy one who lets the hour go by"). (EW)

**v. 18**
- Ellicott: Nebuchadnezzar towers like Tabor (about 1,350 ft above the plain) and Carmel (about 1,805 ft above the sea). (ELL)
- Harrison, quoted by Guzik, says the same. Guzik adds that "As I live" is God's strongest form of oath. (EW)

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: the "daughter" is Egypt personified, packing her bags for a long journey. (ELL)
- The NET Bible translates "poor dear Egypt." (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/jeremiah/46-19.html)

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: the heifer points to Apis worship; "the nation is like its god." "Gadfly" (a stinging fly) is the better reading, and he notes a parallel in the Greek myth of Io. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-46.html)
- Barnes: a gadfly drives oxen mad. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-20.htm)
- Clarke: possibly an allusion to Isis, who was worshipped as a cow. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/46-20.html)
- Coffman: the image is sarcastic, since Memphis was the shrine of the bull. (same URL)
- Pulpit's sermon section draws applications: worldly advantages are no protection, and small troubles can torment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-46.html)

**v. 21**
- Pulpit: the mercenaries were pampered "calves of the stall." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-46.html)
- Thompson, quoted by Guzik: well fed but useless, perhaps fattened for slaughter. (EW)

**v. 22**
- The serpent image is read several ways:
  - Calvin: Egypt will only mutter like a hissing snake, too afraid to complain openly. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/46-22.html)
  - JFB: no longer the bellowing heifer, but a frightened hiss. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-22.htm)
  - Keil & Delitzsch: it is the rustle of a humbled snake among fallen leaves (cf. Isa 29:4), not a fierce hiss. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-23.htm)
  - The NET note says the meaning is debated. (https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Jer&chapter=46&verse=22)
- A mocking dig at Egypt's gods:
  - Harrison, quoted by Guzik: a sarcastic jab at a serpent god used in the royal insignia. (EW)
  - Biblehub's study notes: the cobra on Pharaoh's crown. (https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/46-22.htm)
  - Coffman: the serpent was sacred to a leading Egyptian god. (studylight 46-22 URL above)

**v. 23**
- What is the "forest"?
  - JFB: Egypt's crowded cities, which he numbers at 1,020. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-23.htm)
  - Gill: Egypt's many towns and people; the Targum takes it as her princes. (same URL)
  - The Geneva notes: her great men. (same URL)
- Barnes: Egypt's false worship and wealth must be cleared away like an impassable forest. (same URL)
- What "cannot be searched"? Pulpit and Keil apply it to the enemy's countless numbers, not to how thick the forest is. (same URL)

**v. 24**
- Gill: the Chaldeans are the people of the north. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-24.htm)
- Keil: the picture language is now stated plainly. (same URL)

**v. 25**
- The phrase means "Amon of No." Amon was the chief god of Thebes:
  - Ellicott: possibly a pun on the Hebrew for "multitude." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-25.htm)
  - Barnes: Amon's name means "the concealed." (same URL)
  - Clarke and Constable say the same. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/46-25.html)
- Benson: the Chaldee and Vulgate rendered No as Alexandria, but Alexandria did not exist yet. (biblehub 46-25 URL)
- Calvin takes the word as "multitude." He also makes the point that Jews trusted Egypt as impregnable. (studylight 46-25 URL)
- Keil: "those who trust in him" means the Jews hoping for Egypt's help. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-24.htm)
- Constable: there is as yet no evidence that Nebuchadnezzar reached Thebes. (studylight 46-25 URL)

**v. 26**
- Guzik: God punishes Egypt rather than wiping it out. The same promise of restoration is given to Moab, Ammon and Elam. (EW)
- Coffman: unlike the oracles against Babylon and Nineveh, Egypt's ruin is not permanent, and history bears this out. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/46-26.html)

**vv. 27–28**
- Guzik:
  - The words are aimed at the frightened remnant who fled to Egypt (chs. 42–43).
  - God corrects His people but never makes "a full end" of them.
  - He quotes Clarke (a seed will be kept, and the nation will revive) and Meyer (pruned but not cut down). (EW)
- Keil: an epilogue, prompted by v. 26's warning to "those who trust" in Pharaoh, and in Jeremiah's own style, repeating 30:10–11. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-28.htm)
- Matthew Poole: God punishes His church out of love and "in measure," unlike the wicked. (same URL)
- Gill: the Babylonians are gone, but the Jews still remain a distinct people today. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/46-28.html)
- Matthew Henry: God will not punish them with everlasting destruction. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-20.htm)

---

## 2. Where traditions differ

I found no real denominational dispute over this chapter. The differences are mostly between individual commentators. The tradition labels below are studylight's own; I haven't added any.

- **v. 26: what does the promise to Egypt mean?**
  - Calvin (labelled Calvinist): restoration is not because God is reconciled to Egypt. It shows His mercy even in judging nations and confirms the prophecy. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/46-26.html)
  - Keil & Delitzsch: by comparison with 48:47 and 49:39, it points to the Messianic "last days," not just a later revival. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/46-24.htm)
  - Coffman (labelled Restoration Movement/Arminian): fulfilled in history. (studylight 46-26 URL)
- **vv. 27–28: who is "Jacob," and when is the return?**
  - Smith's Bible Commentary: the yet-future Kingdom Age. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/46-26.html)
  - Gill: Jews preserved as a people to this day. (studylight 46-28 URL)
  - Coffman: God's plan to redeem all mankind through Abraham's line cannot be stopped. (studylight 46-28 URL)
  - Keil: the "true Israel," as opposed to the "rabble" who fled to Egypt. (biblehub 46-28 URL)
  - Clarke (labelled Wesleyan/Methodist, quoted by Guzik): a preserved seed from which the nation revives. (EW)

---

## 3. Other views

- **History and dating (vv. 2, 6, 13):**
  - The Pulpit Commentary reports Ewald's dating after the battle and Niebuhr's alternative dating.
  - It also reports Grote's doubt that Egypt was ever invaded, later answered by Wiedemann's inscription (568–7 BC). (PUL)
  - Constable notes there is still no evidence for an advance on Thebes. (studylight 46-25 URL)
- **Text and ancient translations:**
  - v. 15: the Septuagint reads "Apis."
  - v. 16: the Septuagint reads "Greek sword" and the Vulgate "dove."
  - v. 17: renderings vary across the Septuagint, Vulgate and Luther. (ELL)
  - v. 22: the Septuagint has the serpent "hissing," and Ewald changed the text to match; Keil rejects this. (biblehub 46-23 URL)
  - The Douay-Rheims (Catholic) translates v. 20 as "one that shall goad her." (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/jeremiah/46-20.html) This is only a translation; I didn't read any Catholic commentary.
- **Modern scholarship:** NET's note on v. 22 says the snake image is debated. (classic.net.bible.org URL above)
- Nothing found on Catholic or Orthodox commentary, Bible Odyssey, or prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching.
